headline: BAZ's Dammam and Jeddah Plants Anchor a Localised Cladding Supply Chain
deck: Cold-formed profile sheets, purlins and sandwich panels are a category Saudi Arabia has made domestically since 1978. Local content rules have now caught up with it.
excerpt: Baghlaf Al Zafer, trading as BAZ, has been cold-forming steel in Saudi Arabia since 1978 and produces profile sheets, purlins and insulated sandwich panels from plants in Dammam and Jeddah. Its category is a useful test of what Saudi local content policy can and cannot achieve.
content:
Among the least discussed and most widely used products in Saudi construction is cold-formed steel: the profile sheets, Z and C purlins and insulated sandwich panels that clad and roof almost every warehouse, factory, labour accommodation block and light industrial building in the Kingdom. It is a category Saudi Arabia has manufactured domestically for nearly five decades, and it has become an instructive example of what localisation policy does when the capacity already exists.

Baghlaf Al Zafer, which trades as BAZ, established its first factory in the industrial area of Dammam in 1978 and describes itself as the Kingdom's first commercial steel manufacturer of its type. A second plant followed in Jeddah in 1990, giving the business production on both coasts, and a further factory was opened in Sharjah in 1996. The product range is narrow and deliberate — profile sheets, Z and C purlins, and insulated sandwich panels for roofing and cladding — produced on automated forming lines where consistency of gauge, coating and profile matters more than variety. The company is a member of the Arab Iron and Steel Union and has joined the Made in Saudi programme.

The commercial logic of making these products locally is close to unanswerable. Profile sheet and sandwich panel are geometrically awkward and low in density relative to volume, which makes them expensive to ship and easy to damage in transit. They are also specified late and ordered against a fixed installation window, so a fourteen-week import lead time is not a discount, it is a programme risk. Two coastal plants covering the Eastern Province and the Western Region put most Saudi projects within a day's road haul of a rolling line.

That is why the regulatory changes now working through Saudi procurement land differently in this category than in others. The Local Content and Government Procurement Authority has been raising minimum local content percentages for products on the mandatory list used by government buyers, with a further tranche taking effect from 1 August, and the Made in Saudi programme requires added value of at least 40 percent for the label. Where a domestic industry already operates at scale, those instruments accelerate demand towards plants that can absorb it. Where it does not, they generate paperwork.

The demand side is moving in the right direction for domestic rollformers. Saudi Arabia's industrial build-out is producing exactly the building type this product clads: the Kingdom passed 12,000 factories by the end of 2024 and is targeting 36,000 by 2035, alongside the warehousing and logistics capacity being built out around the ports and industrial cities. Steel demand from the wider construction programme has been strong enough to justify new upstream investment in billet capacity, which over time improves the position of downstream processors who currently buy a share of their coil abroad.

The constraint on this part of the chain is not fabrication capability. It is substrate. Cold-formed products depend on coated steel coil with a specified metallic coating and paint system, and coil quality determines corrosion performance in a coastal, high-humidity environment far more than forming does. A localisation policy that pushes the finished panel into the mandatory list without addressing where the coil comes from moves the import one step upstream rather than removing it.

For buyers walking the halls of Big 5 Construct Saudi this week, the practical questions in this category are unglamorous and worth asking: coating mass, paint system and warranty terms in a marine environment, insulation core and its fire classification against Saudi Building Code requirements, panel span tables against local wind loads, and whether the supplier can deliver a full roof package on a date rather than a lead time. Those are the questions that separate a rollformer from a supplier, and they are the ones a plant inside the Kingdom is best placed to answer.
